slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter twenty-one: the examination of becoming and destruction.

slides.heading: Coming into being, passing away
points: A wave rises and falls; a candle goes out
Things come into being, then pass away
And the stream of lives from death to birth?
slides.say: A wave rises and falls. A candle is lit and goes out. A person is born and, one day, dies. We picture these as things that first come into being and later pass out of it, with a stretch of existing in between. This chapter looks at that pair, coming-into-being and passing-away, and asks how they relate. Can there be a passing-away without a coming-into-being, or the two at once? And what of the stream of lives that Buddhists say runs from one death to the next birth?

slides.heading: The shape of the chapter
points: Brings together chapters 7 and 20
Arising and dissolution: not apart, not together
Real existence forces permanence or annihilation
slides.say: Chapter seven examined arising, abiding and ceasing, and chapter twenty examined how causes produce effects. Chapter twenty-one brings these together. It shows that arising and dissolution cannot be held apart or together if they belong to something that exists on its own. It then answers an objection: does this not leave us with either eternalism or annihilationism? Nagarjuna's reply is that only a belief in real existence forces that choice.

slides.heading: The verses
points: A new translation from the Sanskrit
The Sanskrit is shown above each verse
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: Apart or together?
slides.say: Now the explanation. The first verse states the whole problem. Coming-into-being and passing-away are either found apart from each other or together. Neither works. Passing-away apart from coming-into-being: a wave cannot fall without having risen; death without birth would be the death of nobody. Passing-away together with coming-into-being: a wave cannot rise and fall in the same instant; birth and death are opposites. Coming-into-being apart from passing-away: a wave that rose and never fell would be permanent, but impermanence is never absent from conditioned things. And coming-into-being together with passing-away is the same problem from the other side. Apart, each loses what makes it what it is. Together, opposites share one instant. Verse twenty-one point six draws the conclusion: what cannot be established together or apart cannot be established at all, as things in their own right. Nagarjuna is not saying that waves do not rise and fall. He is saying that arising and dissolution are not two separate events, each existing on its own. They are identified only in relation to each other, and to the thing they are said of.

slides.heading: Does this moment arise or cease?
points: If it arises, it has not yet ceased
If it ceases, it has already arisen
The mind stalls on a 'this moment' doing both
slides.say: Chapter three of The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World turns verse twenty-one point one into a test anyone can try. Does this moment arise or cease? If it arises, it has not yet ceased. If it ceases, it has already arisen. If both, it carries opposites at once. The mind stalls, and it stalls because it is holding on to a this moment that is supposed to do the arising and the ceasing.

slides.heading: Worn away or not
points: 21.7: what wears away does not begin
What is fixed neither begins nor ends
21.8: thing and its rise and fall named together
slides.say: Verse twenty-one point seven tries the same pair on a different axis. Take something that is wearing away, like a burning log. Does it come into being? No: it is already on its way out. Take something fixed. Does it come into being? No: something fixed does not begin. And neither can pass away: the log already passing away does not pass away a second time, and the fixed thing does not pass away at all. Verse eight shows why. Arising and dissolution are not found without a thing that arises and dissolves. And a thing is not found without arising and dissolution: a wave that neither rose nor fell would not be a wave. The thing and its arising and passing are identified together. None of them comes first.

slides.heading: Empty or not, one or different
points: 21.9: no rise and fall for the non-empty, or a blank
21.10: arising and dissolution: not one, not two
21.11: seen, but read through confusion
slides.say: Verse twenty-one point nine says that arising and dissolution make no sense for what is empty, and none for what is not empty. This is the same move as in chapter twenty. A thing with a fixed nature of its own could never arise or end. And if empty is taken as a kind of nothing, a nothing does not arise or end either. Even what is empty in the right sense is not found arising or ending when it is looked for; arising and passing hold as designations. Verse ten adds that arising and dissolution are not one, since rising is not falling, and not two separate things, since each is identified against the other. Then the obvious objection, in verse eleven: but we see things arise and pass away all the time! Nagarjuna answers that they are seen through confusion. He does not mean that change is a hallucination. The seeing is real. The reading of it as the birth and death of self-standing things is the confusion.

slides.heading: Born from what?
slides.say: Verses twelve and thirteen repeat the argument of chapter one, with existence and non-existence as the terms. A thing is not born from a thing: if the result already exists, it needs no birth, and one existing thing does not turn into another without losing its own nature. A thing is not born from a non-thing: nothing comes from nothing. And a non-thing is not born at all: an absence has no birthday. Whichever way thing and non-thing are combined, birth finds no place, once both sides are taken to exist or not exist from their own side. Verse thirteen then restates the opening verse of the whole work: not from itself, not from another, not from both. From where, then?

slides.heading: Permanence or annihilation
slides.say: Now the chapter turns to its main concern. An opponent worries that this analysis leaves nothing. Nagarjuna replies, in verse twenty-one point fourteen, that it is the opposite view, belief in real existence, that leaves us stuck. If a thing exists by its own nature, it must be either permanent or impermanent. If permanent, it never changes: that is eternalism. If impermanent, then at some point what really existed must really cease to exist: that is annihilation. There is no third option for a thing with own-nature. The fork between permanence and annihilation opens only for something that exists from its own side. What is designated in dependence never stood there to last for ever or to be wiped out.

slides.heading: The opponent's stream
points: 21.15: existence as a stream of rise and fall
21.16: each real cause really ends: annihilated
21.17: nirvana would annihilate something real
slides.say: The opponent has an answer, in verse fifteen. Existence, they say, is not one lasting thing but a stream: causes rise and fall, each passing away as its effect arises. The stream is never permanent, because each moment ends, and never annihilated, because each moment is followed by another. This is the Abhidharma's way of avoiding both extremes. Nagarjuna replies, in verse sixteen, that the stream does not escape, as long as its moments really exist. Each cause really ends and never comes back, so each cause is annihilated, moment after moment. A string of real endings is a string of annihilations, however close together they sit. And the end of the stream is worse, says verse seventeen. What exists by its own nature cannot coherently come not to exist; yet the path is supposed to end in nirvana, where the stream of becoming is stilled. On the opponent's view, nirvana would be the annihilation of something real.

slides.heading: The joint between two lives
slides.say: The last verses test the stream at its most important joint: death and rebirth. Buddhists speak of a continuum of becoming that links the last moment of one life to the first moment of the next. Where is the link? If the last moment of the old life has ceased, it is gone, and nothing remains to connect with the new one. If it has not ceased, the old life is still going, and the new one cannot begin. If the first moment is born exactly while the last is ceasing, then the ceasing one and the being-born one are two different things, and the stream is just two moments side by side. Or, if we refuse to separate them, the new being would be born in the very aggregates that are dying. So, says verse twenty-one, the stream of becoming is not found in the past, the present or the future. The continuum is not denied as a convention, but it is not found as a thing that flows.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: Waves still rise and fall; candles go out
A later life may follow from an earlier one
Nothing posited for the extremes to be about
slides.say: Waves still rise and fall. Candles are lit and go out. People are born, grow old and die, and a later life can still be spoken of as following from an earlier one, the way the flame of the last watch of the night follows from the flame of the first. Nothing in this chapter removes the ordinary talk of beginning, ending and continuing. What goes is the picture behind it: a thing with its own nature, which must either last for ever or be wiped out, and a stream made of such things, linked by a real hand-over at each joint. Seen as designated in dependence, there is nothing to be eternal and nothing to be annihilated. This is how Madhyamaka avoids both extremes: not by finding a middle object between them, but by not positing the object that the extremes are about.

slides.heading: Check it now
points: Listen to a sound rise, last, and fade
Look for the instant it began and ceased
Yet it was heard, and its ending was heard too
slides.say: This can be tried with any sound. It rises, it lasts a moment, it fades. Look for the instant it came into being and the instant it ceased. Look for the sound itself, apart from its rising and fading. The questions find no foothold. Yet the sound was heard, and its ending was heard too.

slides.heading: In the books
points: Substrateless World: Chapters 3, 8 and 9
The Logic of Dependency: the eight extremes
Anatta to Emptiness: The Last Refuge of Ontology
slides.say: The two books take up these themes in several places. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World: chapter three, on the question does this moment arise or cease; chapter eight, on death as a conventional designation and the continuum of becoming; and chapter nine, on continuity without persistence and freedom from permanence and annihilation. The bonus article, The Logic of Dependency, turns the eight extremes over. And in The Transition from Anatta to Emptiness, The Last Refuge of Ontology dismantles arising and ceasing, the verb as well as the noun. Links to all of them are on the chapter page.
